title: Giant Beetle Babies Are Eating Blueberry Roots
summary:
Blueberry farmers in North Carolina have a new problem. A giant beetle's babies, called larvae, are eating the roots of blueberry bushes underground.

Scientists at North Carolina State University have now found out which beetle is to blame. It is Prionus imbricornus, a longhorn beetle with very long feelers, called antennae. Its larvae can grow to five inches long, but the grown-up beetles do not eat at all.

Female beetles lay their eggs in the soil near the roots of hardwood trees. After the eggs hatch, the larvae chew on the roots and can eat enough to kill a tree.

North Carolina is the first state to show that this beetle feeds on blueberry bushes. Farmers had seen mystery larvae hurting roots since 2010, but the young beetles were hard to tell apart because they look so much alike.

To solve the puzzle, the team set traps with special scents at six blueberry farms and checked the insects' DNA. The DNA matched Prionus imbricornus by 98 to 99 percent. Knowing the exact pest is the first step toward stopping it.
why_it_matters: Blueberries are a fruit you might eat for breakfast, and finding the pest helps farmers keep growing them.

background_read: Beetles are insects, and many beetles start life as larvae, which are young forms that look very different from the grown-up beetle.
Some beetle larvae live underground and chew on plant roots, which can hurt or kill the plants they feed on.
Scientists study an insect's DNA to tell one kind of beetle from another, even when the young ones look almost the same.
